title: Diffie-Hellman
body:
**Two people who have never met agree on a shared secret over a channel everyone can hear.** 1976,
and the paper that started [[Public Key Cryptography]]. It is not an encryption scheme: nothing is
encrypted and no message is sent. It is *key agreement*, and what it produces is the symmetric key
that [[AES]] then uses.

## The protocol

Public and agreed in advance: a large prime $p$ and a generator $g$ of a large-order subgroup of
$\mathbb{Z}_p^*$.

```
Alice                          public                    Bob
pick a secret  a
                        A = g^a mod p  ------->
                       <-------  B = g^b mod p           pick a secret  b

s = B^a = g^(ba)                                         s = A^b = g^(ab)
```

Both land on $g^{ab} \bmod p$ because exponentiation commutes, $(g^b)^a = (g^a)^b$. The
eavesdropper has $p$, $g$, $g^a$, and $g^b$, and computing $g^{ab}$ from those is the
**computational Diffie-Hellman problem**, which is at most as hard as the
[[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] and believed hard. Nothing secret ever crosses the wire.

```
p = 23, g = 5
a = 6   ->  A = 5^6  mod 23 = 8
b = 15  ->  B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19

Alice: 19^6  mod 23 = 2
Bob:    8^15 mod 23 = 2      shared secret 2
```

The shared value is then run through a [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] (a key derivation function)
to produce an actual key, because $g^{ab}$ is a group element with structure, not a uniform bit
string.

## What it is really doing

Written without mentioning primes, the protocol is: **pick a [[Cyclic Group]], each party raises
the generator to a private exponent, and the shared secret is the generator raised to the
product.** The group is a parameter. Substituting the point group of an elliptic curve gives ECDH,
which is what your browser actually runs, and nothing else in the protocol changes. See
[[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]].

## It has no authentication, and that is fatal

Diffie-Hellman by itself is **completely broken by an active attacker.** Mallory sits in the
middle, runs a separate exchange with each side, and relays:

```
Alice  <--- g^m ---  Mallory  --- g^m --->  Bob
       ---  g^a --->         <--- g^b ---
```

Alice shares a key with Mallory, Bob shares a different key with Mallory, and Mallory decrypts,
reads, re-encrypts, and forwards. Neither endpoint sees anything wrong. The mathematics cannot
distinguish the cases, because both exchanges are perfectly valid; the fix has to come from
outside, by **signing** the exchanged values with a key whose ownership is already established.
That is [[Digital Signature]] plus certificates, and it is the standing example of the point made
in [[Public Key Cryptography]]: the maths solves confidentiality, not identity.

## Ephemeral DH and forward secrecy

Generate a fresh $a$ and $b$ for every session and discard them afterwards (**DHE** / **ECDHE**).
Then the session key was never derived from any long-term key, so an attacker who records the
traffic today and steals the server's private key in five years still cannot decrypt it. That
property is **forward secrecy**, it is why static RSA key transport was removed from TLS 1.3, and
it is the main practical reason Diffie-Hellman is preferred over encrypting a session key with
[[RSA]].

Two implementation rules worth carrying:

- Use a **safe prime** $p = 2q+1$ and work in the order-$q$ subgroup, so Pohlig-Hellman has nothing
  to chew on. Weak or shared small groups gave the Logjam attack.
- Validate the received value. Accepting $A = 0$ or $A = 1$ makes the shared secret trivially
  known, and small-subgroup confinement attacks leak the private exponent one bit at a time.
